Thank you for submitting your article "Ensemble cryo-EM uncovers inchworm-like translocation of a viral IRES through the ribosome" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by John Kuriyan (Senior editor) and three reviewers, one of whom, Sriram Subramaniam, is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

Type IV internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs) initiate translation without using any of the canonical eukaryotic translation initiation factors. Thus, they represent the most streamlined mode of eukaryotic translation initiation discovered. They have been studied biochemically and structurally. The current prevailing model is that these IRESs fold into a compact 2-domain structure that bind to the 40S subunit through multiple contacts. Critical interactions occur between two IRES RNA stem-loops and the head of the 40S subunit. This positions one of the IRES domains into the decoding groove. This domain (a pseudoknot, PKI) mimics the tRNA-mRNA anticodon-codon interaction, apparently first docking in the A site. The 60S subunit then joins in a GTP hydrolysis-independent step. This complex is then recognized by elongation factor 2, which catalyzes translocation of the PKI domain into the P site, allowing tRNA delivery to the A-site. Another round of translocation brings this tRNA to the P site. The mechanisms of these IRESs suggests that they can be powerful tools for understand translation in general (a feature the authors of this manuscript exploit).

A rich set of biochemical and functional data have established that different parts of the IRES affect different steps, have shown similarities and differences between different type IV IRESs, and have established some of the key differences between the canonical and IRES-driven initiation mechanisms. In addition, various structures of the IRES alone or bound to the ribosome have been published, using both crystallography and cryo-EM. Until recently, the cryo-EM structures were of low-or mid-resolution. However, when combined with the higher resolution data from crystal structures and the many functional and biochemical studies, the models that resulted have been very informative and have allowed many predictions to be made.

In this manuscript, the authors attack the question of IRES translocation. They present a series of cryo-EM structures of a Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV) IRES bound to 80S and eEF2, using the antibiotic sordarin. The authors interpret the set of structures as showing the trajectory of the mRNA-tRNA-mimicking PKI moving from the A to the P site. Overall, this is an impressive piece of work. It appears technically well done, the description is rich and detailed, and the conclusions are well supported and discussed. As such, it represents an important addition to the IRES field. In many ways, the mechanism that is presented is not surprising; an "inchworm"- like mechanism has been predicted in the literature (although never referred to as such!). However, to see it and to have detailed structures along the trajectory is very important. I will say that as the paper is written, it probably speaks as much to the mechanism of eEF2 and translocation in general as it does to IRES-specific function.

Essential revisions:

1) There are few recent discoveries regarding IRES function that are not mentioned in the manuscript. As these discoveries relate directly to the interactions that the authors visualize and discuss, they should add a bit of discussion or analysis:

• First, some type IV IRESs to can initiate in an alternate reading frame. Do their structures suggest how this might occur? This effect appears to relate to a base adjacent to the codon-anticodon mimic, which they have good density for. References: Au et al. (2015) PNAS 112:E6446-55, Wang et al. (2014) PloS One 9:e103601, Ren et al. (2012) PNAS 109:E630-9, Ren et al. (2014) Nucleic Acids Res. 42:9366-82.

• Recent work implicates the VLR loop/loop 3 in PKI as having a role in eEF2 function: Ruehle et al., (2015) eLife), and it has been explored in manuscripts from the Jan lab. This is not mentioned or discussed. Can the authors comment on what this loop is doing and contacting and does it explain this previous work? Also, the Ruehle et al. presents biochemical data in favor of their spontaneous forward and reverse translocation that the authors allude to.

2) The interactions between the highly conserved apical loops of SL4 and 5 make critical interactions with eS5 and eS25. In addition, the IRES makes critical interaction with the L1 stalk. These regions of the type IV IRESs are very highly conserved, but no high-resolution information is known for these interactions. Was the local resolution good enough to say how binding these mysterious interactions are achieved, and perhaps how it relates to ribosome conformation, IRES conformation, etc.?

3) Related to the above, it would be interesting to see some more details of how the IRES changes conformation; not just globally, but internally. Is the resolution sufficient to see this? Any mechanistic insight?

4) By the very nature of this work, in which 5 structures at near atomic resolution are dissected, the figures are quite dense in information content and individual panels are generally quite small. In addition, the paper is quite long because of the high information content. The general reader can of course skip the detailed sections in the middle and read the Discussion, which is very clear. What seems to be missing for a general reader who wishes to dive into the "information forest" is an outline figure at the beginning that shows the ribosome translation cycle with various subunit motions and tRNA movements indicated. This would certainly help those who do not work in the ribosome field.

claims.source: eEF2 settles into the A site from Structure I to V, as the tip of domain IV shifts by ~10 Å relative to the body and by ~20 Å relative to the swiveling head.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claims.claim: From Structure I to V, domains II and III of eEF2 migrate by ~10 Å along the 40S surface.
claims.source: From Structure I to V, these central domains migrate by ~10 Å along the 40S surface (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6c.

claims.claim: In Structure V, domain III is displaced as a result of interaction with uS12.
claims.source: Comparison of eEF2 conformations reveals that in Structure V, domain III is displaced as a result of interaction with uS12, as discussed below.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and elaborated later.

claims.claim: In Structure I, PKI is shifted toward the P site by ~3 Å relative to its position in the initiation complex.
claims.source: In the fully rotated Structure I, PKI is shifted toward the P site by ~3 Å relative to its position in the initiation complex but maintains interactions with the partially swiveled head.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claims.claim: C1274 of the 18S rRNA base pairs with the first nucleotide of the ORF immediately downstream of PKI.
claims.source: At the head, C1274 of the 18S rRNA (C1054 in E. coli) base pairs with the first nucleotide of the ORF immediately downstream of PKI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: C1274 provides a stacking platform for the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI and is defined as the foundation of the 'head A site'.
claims.source: The C1274:G6953 base pair provides a stacking platform for the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI. We therefore define C1274 as the foundation of the 'head A site'.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a definition based on structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure I, PKI does not contact the decoding-center nucleotides G577, A1755 and A1756.
claims.source: In Structure I, PKI does not contact these nucleotides (Figures 2g and 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2g and 7.

claims.claim: The position of eEF2 on the 40S subunit of Structure I is markedly distinct from those in Structures II to V.
claims.source: The position of eEF2 on the 40S subunit of Structure I is markedly distinct from those in Structures II to V.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure I, the translocase interacts with the 40S body but does not contact the head.
claims.source: The translocase interacts with the 40S body but does not contact the head (Figures 5b and 6a; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 5b and 6a.

claims.claim: In Structure I, domain IV is partially engaged with the body A site.
claims.source: Domain IV is partially engaged with the body A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: The tip of domain IV is wedged between PKI and decoding-center nucleotides A1755 and A1756 in Structure I.
claims.source: The tip of domain IV is wedged between PKI and decoding-center nucleotides A1755 and A1756, which are bulged out of h44.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The tip of domain IV contains the histidine-diphthamide triad (H583, H694 and Diph699).
claims.source: This tip contains the histidine-diphthamide triad (H583, H694 and Diph699), which interacts with the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI and A1756 (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: Histidines 583 and 694 interact with the phosphate backbone of the anticodon-like strand at G6907 and C6908.
claims.source: Histidines 583 and 694 interact with the phosphate backbone of the anticodon-like strand (at G6907 and C6908).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: Diphthamide is a unique posttranslational modification conserved in archaeal and eukaryotic EF2.
claims.source: Diphthamide is a unique posttranslational modification conserved in archaeal and eukaryotic EF2 (at residue 699 in S. cerevisiae) and involves addition of a ~7-Å long 3-carboxyamido-3-(trimethylamino)-propyl moiety to the histidine imidazole ring at CE1.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a definition based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The trimethylamino end of Diph699 packs over A1756 in Structure I.
claims.source: The trimethylamino end of Diph699 packs over A1756 (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: The histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 replaces the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI in comparison with the initiation state.
claims.source: Thus, in comparison with the initiation state, the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 replaces the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The conformation of the eEF2 GTPase center in Structure I resembles that of a GTP-bound translocase.
claims.source: Unlike in Structures II to V, the conformation of the eEF2 GTPase center in Structure I resembles that of a GTP-bound translocase (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5e.

claims.claim: Switch loop II carries the catalytic H108.
claims.source: Switch loop II (aa 105–110), which carries the catalytic H108 (H92 in E. coli EF-G; (Cunha et al., 2013; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Koripella et al., 2015; Salsi et al., 2014) is well resolved in all five structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Switch loop I is resolved only in Structure I.
claims.source: By contrast, switch loop I (aa 50–70 in S. cerevisiae eEF2) is resolved only in Structure I (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The conformations of SWI and the GTPase center in Structure I are similar to those observed in ribosome-bound EF-Tu and EF-G in the presence of GTP analogs.
claims.source: As such, the conformations of SWI and the GTPase center in general are similar to those observed in ribosome-bound EF-Tu (Voorhees et al., 2010) and EF-G (Pulk and Cate, 2013; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013) in the presence of GTP analogs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: In Structure II, PKI is further shifted along the 40S body, traversing ~4 Å toward the P site relative to Structure I.
claims.source: In Structure II, relative to Structure I, PKI is further shifted along the 40S body, traversing ~4 Å toward the P site (Figures 2e, f, and g), while stacking on C1274 at the head A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2e, f, and g.

claims.claim: The intermediate position of PKI in Structure II is possible due to a large swivel of the head relative to the body.
claims.source: Thus, the intermediate position of PKI is possible due to a large swivel of the head relative to the body, which brings the head A site close to the body P site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure II, domain IV of eEF2 is further entrenched in the A site by ~3 Å relative to the body and ~8 Å relative to the head.
claims.source: Domain IV of eEF2 is further entrenched in the A site by ~3 Å relative to the body and ~8 Å relative to the head, preserving its interactions with PKI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claims.claim: In Structure II, the decoding center residues A1755 and A1756 are rearranged to pack inside helix 44.
claims.source: The decoding center residues A1755 and A1756 are rearranged to pack inside helix 44, making room for eEF2.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure III, PKI has translocated along the 40S body to the body P site.
claims.source: The map allows placement of PKI at the body P site (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Thus, in Structure III, PKI has translocated along the 40S body, but the head remains fully swiveled so that PKI is between the head A and P sites.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Lower resolution of the map in Structure III suggests that PKI is somewhat destabilized in the vicinity of the body P site.
claims.source: Lower resolution of the map in this region suggests that PKI is somewhat destabilized in the vicinity of the body P site in the absence of stacking with the foundations of the head A site (C1274) or P site (U1191).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the map quality.

claims.claim: In Structure IV, the 40S subunit is almost non-rotated relative to the 60S subunit, and the 40S head is mid-swiveled.
claims.source: In Structure IV, the 40S subunit is almost non-rotated relative to the 60S subunit, and the 40S head is mid-swiveled.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claims.claim: In Structure IV, unwinding of the head moves the head P-site residue U1191 and body P-site residue C1637 closer together.
claims.source: Unwinding of the head moves the head P-site residue U1191 and body P-site residue C1637 closer together, resulting in a partially restored 40S P site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure IV, PKI is partially accommodated in the P site.
claims.source: Whereas C1637 forms a stacking platform for the last base pair of PKI, U1191 does not yet stack on PKI because the head remains partially swiveled. This renders PKI partially accommodated in the P site (Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2g.

claims.claim: In Structure IV, unwinding of the 40S head positions the head A site closer to the body A site.
claims.source: Unwinding of the 40S head also positions the head A site closer to the body A site. This results in rearrangements of eEF2 interactions with the head, allowing eEF2 to advance further into the A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, PKI is fully accommodated in the P site.
claims.source: In the nearly non-rotated and non-swiveled ribosome conformation in Structure V closely resembling that of the post-translocation 80S•2tRNA•mRNA complex (Svidritskiy et al., 2014), PKI is fully accommodated in the P site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, the codon-anticodon–like helix of PKI is stacked on P-site residues U1191 and C1637.
claims.source: The codon-anticodon–like helix is stacked on P-site residues U1191 and C1637 (Figure 3d), analogous to stacking of the tRNA-mRNA helix (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 3d and 3e.

claims.claim: In Structure V, protein uS12 is shifted along with the 40S body as a result of intersubunit rotation.
claims.source: In Structure V, protein uS12 is shifted along with the 40S body as a result of intersubunit rotation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, uS12 forms extensive interactions with eEF2 domains II and III.
claims.source: In this position, uS12 forms extensive interactions with eEF2 domains II and III. Specifically, the C-terminal tail of uS12 packs against the β-barrel of domain II, while the β-barrel of uS12 packs against helix A of domain III.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, the tip of helix A of domain III is shifted by ~5 Å relative to that in Structure I.
claims.source: This shifts the tip of helix A of domain III (at aa 500) by ~5 Å (relative to that in Structure I) toward domain I.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural measurements.

claims.claim: In Structure V, domain IV of eEF2 is fully accommodated in the A site.
claims.source: Domain IV of eEF2 is fully accommodated in the A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, the first codon of the open reading frame is positioned in the A site.
claims.source: The first codon of the open reading frame is also positioned in the A site, with bases exposed toward eEF2 (Figure 7), resembling the conformations of the A-site codons in EF-G-bound 70S complexes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: In Structure V, the histidine-diphthamide tip is bound in the minor groove of the P-site codon-anticodon helix.
claims.source: As in the preceding Structures, the histidine-diphthamide tip is bound in the minor groove of the P-site codon-anticodon helix.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: In Structure V, Diph699 interacts with four out of six codon-anticodon nucleotides.
claims.source: Diph699 slightly rearranges, relative to that in Structure I (Figure 7), and interacts with four out of six codon-anticodon nucleotides.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: The structures represent the trajectory of eEF2-induced IRES translocation.
claims.source: We propose that together with the previously reported initiation state (Koh et al., 2014), these structures represent the trajectory of eEF2-induced IRES translocation (shown as an animation in http://labs.umassmed.edu/korostelevlab/msc/iresmovie.gif and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Translocation of the TSV IRES on the 40S subunit globally resembles a step of an inchworm.
claims.source: Translocation of the TSV IRES on the 40S subunit globally resembles a step of an inchworm (Figure 4; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 4.

claims.claim: At all steps of IRES translocation, the head of the IRES inchworm (L1.1 region) is supported by the mobile L1 stalk.
claims.source: Notably, at all steps, the head of the IRES inchworm (L1.1 region) is supported by the mobile L1 stalk.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: Upon translocation, the GCU start codon is positioned in the A site, ready for interaction with Ala-tRNAAla upon eEF2 departure.
claims.source: Upon translocation, the GCU start codon is positioned in the A site (Structure V), ready for interaction with Ala-tRNAAla upon eEF2 departure.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The presence of several translocation complexes in a single sample suggests that the structures represent equilibrium states of forward and reverse translocation of the IRES.
claims.source: The presence of several translocation complexes in a single sample suggests that the structures represent equilibrium states of forward and reverse translocation of the IRES, which interconvert among each other.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Intergenic IRESs are prone to reverse translocation.
claims.source: This is consistent with the observations that the intergenic IRESs are prone to reverse translocation. Specifically, biochemical toe-printing studies in the presence of eEF2•GTP identified IRES in a non-translocated position unless eEF1a•aa-tRNA is also present (Jan et al., 2003; Pestova and Hellen, 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claims.claim: IRES translocation by eEF2 is futile: the IRES returns to the A site upon releasing eEF2•GDP unless an amino-acyl tRNA enters the A site.
claims.source: These findings indicate that IRES translocation by eEF2 is futile: the IRES returns to the A site upon releasing eEF2•GDP unless an amino-acyl tRNA enters the A site and blocks IRES back-translocation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of prior biochemical studies.

claims.claim: Intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site.
claims.source: Specifically, intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site, while the head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
claims.source: Specifically, intersubunit rotation allows eEF2 entry into the A site, while the head swivel mediates PKI translocation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Reverse intersubunit rotation facilitates full docking of eEF2 in the A site.
claims.source: Reverse intersubunit rotation from Structure I to V shifts the translocation tunnel (the tunnel between the A, P and E sites) toward eEF2, which is rigidly attached to the 60S subunit. This allows eEF2 to move into the A site. As such, reverse intersubunit rotation facilitates full docking of eEF2 in the A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: eEF2 appears to directly force PKI out of the A site.
claims.source: Because the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 (H583, H694 and Diph699) attaches to the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI, eEF2 appears to directly force PKI out of the A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The fully swiveled conformations of Structures II and III represent the mid-point of translocation.
claims.source: The fully swiveled conformations of Structures II and III represent the mid-point of translocation, in which PKI relocates between the head A site and body P site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The structures provide the first high-resolution view of the dynamics of a ribosomal translocase inferred from an ensemble of structures sampled under uniform conditions.
claims.source: To our knowledge, our work provides the first high-resolution view of the dynamics of a ribosomal translocase that is inferred from an ensemble of structures sampled under uniform conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a claim about the novelty of the work.

claims.claim: The first role of eEF2 in translocation is to directly shift PKI out of the A site upon spontaneous reverse intersubunit rotation.
claims.source: As discussed above, the first role is to directly shift PKI out of the A site upon spontaneous reverse intersubunit rotation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The tip of domain IV docks next to PKI, with diphthamide 699 fit into the minor groove of the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI.
claims.source: In our structures, the tip of domain IV docks next to PKI, with diphthamide 699 fit into the minor groove of the codon-anticodon-like helix of PKI (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: This arrangement rationalizes inactivation of eEF2 by diphtheria toxin.
claims.source: This arrangement rationalizes inactivation of eEF2 by diphtheria toxin, which catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the diphthamide (reviewed in Collier, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claims.claim: The bulky ADP-ribosyl moiety at the NE2 position would disrupt the interaction of diphthamide with PKI, rendering eEF2 unable to bind to the A site.
claims.source: The enzyme ADP-ribosylates the NE2 atom of the imidazole ring, which in our structures interacts with the first two residues of the anticodon-like strand of PKI. The bulky ADP-ribosyl moiety at this position would disrupt the interaction, rendering eEF2 unable to bind to the A site (Nygard and Nilsson, 1990) and/or stalled on ribosomes in a non-productive conformation (Bermek, 1976; Davydova and Ovchinnikov, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claims.claim: Positively-charged patches of eEF2 slide over rRNA of the 40S body and head.
claims.source: Positively-charged patches of domains II and III (R391, K394, R433, R510) and IV (K613, R617, R609, R631, K651) slide over rRNA of the 40S body (h5) and head (h18 and h33/h34), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: Sliding of eEF2 involves reorganization of electrostatic, perhaps isoenergetic interactions.
claims.source: Thus, sliding of eEF2 involves reorganization of electrostatic, perhaps isoenergetic interactions, echoing those implied in extraordinarily fast ribosome inactivation rates by the small-protein ribotoxins (Korennykh et al., 2006) and in fast protein association and diffusion along DNA (Givaty and Levy, 2009; Gorman et al., 2010; Halford, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claims.claim: The second key function of the translocase is 'unlocking' of intrasubunit rearrangements required for step-wise translocation of PKI on the small subunit.
claims.source: Comparison of our structures with the 80S•IRES initiation structure reveals the structural basis for the second key function of the translocase: 'unlocking' of intrasubunit rearrangements that are required for step-wise translocation of PKI on the small subunit.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: eEF2 induces head swivel by 'unlocking' the head-body interactions.
claims.source: Our structures suggest that eEF2 induces head swivel by 'unlocking' the head-body interactions (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: The histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 is wedged between A1755 and A1756 and PKI at an early pre-translocation step.
claims.source: Structure I demonstrates that at an early pre-translocation step, the histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 is wedged between A1755 and A1756 and PKI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data from Structure I.

claims.claim: Destabilization of PKI at the body A site allows PKI to detach from the body A site upon spontaneous reverse 40S body rotation.
claims.source: This destabilization allows PKI to detach from the body A site upon spontaneous reverse 40S body rotation, while maintaining interactions with the head A site.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The histidine-diphthamide-induced disengagement of PKI from A1755 and A1756 provides the structural definition for the 'unlocking' mode of eEF2 action.
claims.source: The histidine-diphthamide-induced disengagement of PKI from A1755 and A1756 therefore provides the structural definition for the 'unlocking' mode of eEF2 action.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Both PKI and eEF2 passively migrate into the P and A site, respectively, during spontaneous 40S body rotation and head swivel.
claims.source: In summary, our structures are consistent with a model of eEF2-induced translocation in which both PKI and eEF2 passively migrate into the P and A site, respectively, during spontaneous 40S body rotation and head swivel, the latter being allowed by 'unlocking' of the A site by eEF2.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Thermal fluctuations of the 40S head domain are sufficient for translocation along the energetically flat trajectory.
claims.source: Observation of different PKI conformations sampling a range of positions between the A and P sites in the presence of eEF2•GDP implies that thermal fluctuations of the 40S head domain are sufficient for translocation along the energetically flat trajectory.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: In the fully-rotated pre-translocation-like Structure I, switch loop I interacts with helix 14 of the 18S rRNA.
claims.source: In the fully-rotated pre-translocation-like Structure I, an additional interaction exists. Here, switch loop I interacts with helix 14 (415CAAA418) of the 18S rRNA.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural data.

claims.claim: The fully rotated 40S subunit of the pre-translocation ribosome provides an interaction surface for binding of the GTP-bound translocase.
claims.source: We conclude that unlike other conformations of the ribosome, the fully rotated 40S subunit of the pre-translocation ribosome provides an interaction surface, complementing the P stalk and SRL, for binding of the GTP-bound translocase.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The shift of domain III by uS12 initiates intra-domain rearrangements in eEF2.
claims.source: We propose that the shift of domain III by uS12 initiates intra-domain rearrangements in eEF2, which unstack the β-platform of domain III from that of domain V.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Structure V captures a 'pre-unstacking' state due to stabilization of the interface between domains III and V by sordarin.
claims.source: As we discuss below, Structure V captures a 'pre-unstacking' state due to stabilization of the interface between domains III and V by sordarin.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Density maps clearly show GDP and Mg2+ in each structure.
claims.source: Although our complex was assembled using eEF2•GTP, density maps clearly show GDP and Mg2+ in each structure (Figure 5g).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 5g.

claims.claim: Sordarin stalls eEF2 on the ribosome in the GDP-bound form, i.e. following GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
claims.source: Our structures therefore indicate that sordarin stalls eEF2 on the ribosome in the GDP-bound form, i.e. following GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: Sordarin acts to prevent full reverse rotation and release of eEF2•GDP by stabilizing the interdomain interface.
claims.source: We propose that sordarin acts to prevent full reverse rotation and release of eEF2•GDP by stabilizing the interdomain interface and thus blocking uS12-induced disengagement of domain III from domain V.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: tRNA and IRES translocations occur via the same general trajectory.
claims.source: First, we propose that tRNA and IRES translocations occur via the same general trajectory.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The intermediate locations of the elusive A-to-P-site translocating tRNA are similar to those of PKI in our structures.
claims.source: Overall, these correlations suggest that the intermediate locations of the elusive A-to-P-site translocating tRNA are similar to those of PKI in our structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior work.

claims.claim: Unlocking involves separation of the codon-anticodon helix from the decoding center residues by the protruding tip of eEF2/EF-G.
claims.source: Unlocking involves separation of the codon-anticodon helix from the decoding center residues by the protruding tip of eEF2/EF-G (Figure 7), occurring in the fully rotated ribosome at an early pre-translocation step.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 7.

claims.claim: The head swivel brings the head A site to the body P site, allowing a step-wise conveying of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
claims.source: In addition to the 'gate-opening' role, we now show that the head swivel brings the head A site to the body P site, allowing a step-wise conveying of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The similar populations of particles in the reconstructions suggest that the intermediate translocation states sample several energetically similar and interconverting conformations.
claims.source: Finally, the similar populations of particles (within a 2X range) in our 80S•IRES•eEF2 reconstructions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggest that the intermediate translocation states sample several energetically similar and interconverting conformations.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The energy landscape of translocation is not completely flat and contains local minima for transient positions of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
claims.source: Our findings implicate, however, that the energy landscape is not completely flat and contains local minima for transient positions of the codon-anticodon helix between the A and P sites.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The TSV IRES structurally and dynamically represents a chimera of the 2tRNA•mRNA translocating complex.
claims.source: The cryo-EM structures demonstrate that the TSV IRES structurally and dynamically represents a chimera of the 2tRNA•mRNA translocating complex (A/P-tRNA • P/E-tRNA • mRNA).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The IRES lacks three out of six tRNA-like domains involved in tRNA translocation.
claims.source: A large structural difference between the IRES and the 2tRNA•mRNA complex exists, however, in that the IRES lacks three out of six tRNA-like domains involved in tRNA translocation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: The uniformity of ribosome dynamics underscores the idea that translocation is an inherent and structurally-optimized property of the ribosome.
claims.source: The uniformity of ribosome dynamics underscores the idea that translocation is an inherent and structurally-optimized property of the ribosome, supported also by translocation activity in the absence of the elongation factor.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data in the context of prior knowledge.

claims.claim: Intergenic IRESs represent a striking example of convergent molecular evolution.
claims.source: Intergenic IRESs, in turn, represent a striking example of convergent molecular evolution.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Viral mRNAs have evolved to adopt an atypical structure to employ the inherent ribosome dynamics.
claims.source: Viral mRNAs have evolved to adopt an atypical structure to employ the inherent ribosome dynamics, to be able to hijack the host translational machinery in a simple fashion.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: 80S ribosomes used in this study were prepared from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303.
claims.source: 80S ribosomes used in this study were prepared from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain W303 as described previously (Ben-Shem et al., 2011; Koh et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claims.claim: C-terminally His6-tagged eEF2 was produced in yeast TKY675 cells.
claims.source: C-terminally His6-tagged eEF2 was produced in yeast TKY675 cells obtained from Terri Goss Kinzy.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claims.claim: Cryo-EM data were collected in movie mode on an FEI Krios microscope operating at 300 kV.
claims.source: Cryo-EM data were collected in movie mode on an FEI Krios microscope (FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a K2 Summit direct detector (Gatan Inc., Pleasanton, CA) operating in super-resolution mode with pixel size of 0.82 Å per super-resolution pixel.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claims.claim: 1,105,737 two-dimensional images of ribosomes were picked automatically.
claims.source: 1,105,737 two-dimensional images of ribosomes (termed 'particles') were picked automatically, extracted into 256 x 256 boxes and converted to MRC/CCP4 format with a corresponding list of micrograph numbers and defocus values for input to FREALIGN v9 (Lyumkis et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claims.claim: FREALIGN v9 was used for refinement, classification and 3D reconstruction of all ribosome structures.
claims.source: FREALIGN v9 was used for refinement, classification and 3D reconstruction of all ribosome structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claims.claim: The structures have average resolutions of 3.5 to 4.2 Å.
claims.source: This approach revealed five 80S•IRES•eEF2•GDP structures at average resolutions of 3.5 to 4.2 Å, sufficient to locate IRES domains and to resolve individual residues in the core regions of the ribosome and eEF2 (Figures 3c,d, and 5f,h; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), including the post-translational modification diphthamide 699 (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section.

results.result: Five distinct ribosome structures (I-V) were obtained from a single cryo-EM specimen using maximum-likelihood classification, representing different translocation intermediates with PKI positioned between the A and P sites (Structures I-IV) or fully in the P site (Structure V). The structures were resolved at 3.5-4.2 Å resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C25-C30, and C150 collectively demonstrate that five structures were obtained from a single specimen using appropriate cryo-EM methods and computational classification. The structural data showing PKI in different positions (C27-C30) and the resolution measurements (C150) provide strong evidence for capturing translocation intermediates. The methodology is well-documented in the Materials and Methods section.

results.result: The IRES undergoes inchworm-like translocation, rearranging from extended to compact to extended conformations as PKI moves from the A to P site. The distance between PKI and SL4 changes from ~50 Å (initiation) to ~35 Å (Structures I-II) to ~25 Å (Structures III-IV) and back to ~45 Å (Structure V), while the L1.1 region remains anchored to the L1 stalk throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C41-C44, C101-C103 are strongly supported by structural measurements showing systematic changes in IRES conformation and inter-domain distances across the five structures. The inchworm-like mechanism is well-documented through quantitative distance measurements and structural comparisons shown in Figures 3 and 4.

results.result: Intersubunit rotation decreases progressively from Structure I (~10° rotation) through Structures II-III (~5°), Structure IV (~1°), to Structure V (~0.5°), representing reverse rotation of the 40S body relative to the 60S subunit. This reverse rotation facilitates eEF2 entry into the A site by shifting the translocation tunnel toward the 60S-attached eEF2.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35, C108, and C110 are supported by quantitative angular measurements documented in Figure 2 and structural alignments. The progressive decrease in rotation angle is well-characterized, and the mechanistic interpretation linking rotation to eEF2 entry is consistent with the structural data showing eEF2 rigidly attached to the 60S subunit.

results.result: The 40S head undergoes swiveling that is maximal in mid-rotated Structures II and III (17°), with intermediate swiveling in Structures I (12°) and IV (14°), and minimal swiveling in Structure V (1°). This head swivel mediates PKI translocation by bringing the head A site close to the body P site, and requires eEF2 for induction or stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38, C109, C112, and C137 are supported by angular measurements in Figure 2 and structural comparisons. The correlation between maximum head swivel and PKI transitioning between sites is well-documented. The requirement for eEF2 is supported by comparison with eEF2-free structures showing less swivel (C38).

results.result: eEF2 remains rigidly attached to the GTPase-associated center (P stalk and sarcin-ricin loop) of the 60S subunit throughout translocation, with the P stalk shifted ~13 Å toward the A site compared to eEF2-free structures. Domain IV of eEF2 gradually enters the A site through 40S rotation and head swivel, shifting ~10 Å relative to the body and ~20 Å relative to the head from Structure I to V, while domains II-III migrate ~10 Å along the 40S surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C54-C58, C60-C63 are strongly supported by structural data showing consistent eEF2-60S interactions and quantitative measurements of domain movements. The rigid attachment to the 60S and passive sliding mechanism are well-documented through RMSD measurements (≤2.5 Å for P stalk, ≤2 Å for eEF2 global conformation) and distance measurements across structures.

results.result: The histidine-diphthamide tip of eEF2 domain IV (H583, H694, Diph699) wedges between PKI and decoding center nucleotides A1755/A1756 in Structure I, separating PKI from these nucleotides and 'unlocking' the A site. This disengagement allows PKI to detach from the body A site while maintaining head A site interactions, facilitating head swivel and PKI translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C68, C72-C74, C76-C77, C115, C120-C124, and C136 are strongly supported by high-resolution structural data in Figure 7 showing specific interactions between the diphthamide tip and PKI/decoding center. The 'unlocking' mechanism is well-defined structurally, showing how eEF2 disrupts PKI-decoding center contacts that stabilize the initiation state.

results.result: All five structures contain eEF2 bound with GDP (not GTP) and sordarin, despite complex assembly with eEF2•GTP. Density maps clearly show GDP and Mg2+ in the GTPase center, indicating that sordarin stalls eEF2 on the ribosome in the GDP-bound form following GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C52-C53, C131-C132 are supported by clear cryo-EM density for GDP shown in Figure 5. The interpretation that GTP hydrolysis occurred before structure capture is reasonable given the experimental design and density evidence, though the timing of hydrolysis relative to translocation steps cannot be definitively determined from these static structures.

results.result: Structure I shows eEF2 in a GTP-like conformation with switch loop I resolved and interacting with helix 14 of 18S rRNA, similar to GTP-bound translational GTPases. This interaction is unique to the fully rotated 40S subunit and is absent in Structures II-V where switch loop I is unresolved, suggesting that the fully rotated pre-translocation ribosome provides a specific binding surface for GTP-bound translocase.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81, C127-C128 are supported by structural data showing switch loop I density only in Structure I (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and its interaction with h14. The comparison with GTP-analog-bound structures is appropriate. However, the interpretation is complicated by the presence of GDP rather than GTP in all structures, suggesting Structure I may represent a post-hydrolysis state that retains GTP-like conformation.

results.result: PKI progressively translocates from the A site through intermediate positions in Structures I-IV to full P-site accommodation in Structure V. In Structure I, PKI is shifted ~3 Å from initiation position while maintaining head A site contact. In Structures II-IV, PKI occupies intermediate positions between head A and body P sites, facilitated by head swivel. In Structure V, PKI is fully accommodated with its codon-anticodon-like helix stacked on P-site residues U1191 and C1637.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C93 describing PKI positions in Structures I-V are well-supported by structural data and distance measurements shown in Figures 2 and 3. The progressive translocation is documented through quantitative measurements and structural comparisons. The interpretation of intermediate states is reasonable given the structural evidence, though the lower resolution of Structure III (C87) introduces some uncertainty about PKI positioning in that state.

results.result: In Structure V, protein uS12 shifts with the 40S body during reverse rotation and forms extensive interactions with eEF2 domains II-III, causing a ~5 Å shift of domain III helix A tip toward domain I. This represents a 'pre-unstacking' state where sordarin stabilizes the domain III-V interface, potentially blocking the domain separation required for eEF2 release.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96, C64, C129-C130 are supported by structural data showing uS12-eEF2 interactions and domain III displacement in Structure V. The measurements are quantitative and well-documented. However, the 'pre-unstacking' interpretation (C129-C130) is somewhat speculative as it proposes a mechanism for eEF2 release that is not directly observed in the structures.

results.result: Sordarin prevents full reverse rotation and eEF2•GDP release by stabilizing the interdomain interface between domains III and V, blocking uS12-induced disengagement of these domains.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 proposes a mechanism for sordarin action based on structural observations, but this is largely speculative. While the structures show sordarin binding between domains III and V, and Structure V shows uS12 interaction with domain III, the claim that sordarin blocks domain separation and prevents eEF2 release is an inference not directly demonstrated by the data. Additional experiments would be needed to validate this mechanism.

results.result: The 5' domain of the IRES maintains contacts with the ribosome through L1.1, SL4, and SL5 in Structures I-IV, but in Structure V, SL5 becomes mobile (missing density) and SL4 shifts ~20 Å. Loop 3 of PKI is poorly resolved in Structures I-IV but becomes ordered in Structure V, binding in the E site and interacting with uS7, suggesting it stabilizes the post-translocation state.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40, C45-C48 are supported by cryo-EM density observations and structural comparisons shown in Figures 3 and supplementary figures. The interpretation of missing/weak density as indicating mobility is standard practice in cryo-EM. The ordering of loop 3 in Structure V and its proposed stabilizing role is supported by structural data and consistent with prior biochemical studies cited.

results.result: In Structure V, domain IV of eEF2 is fully accommodated in the A site with the first ORF codon positioned in the A site. The histidine-diphthamide tip remains bound in the minor groove of the P-site codon-anticodon helix, with Diph699 interacting with four of six codon-anticodon nucleotides.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by structural data in Figure 7 showing domain IV and codon positioning in Structure V. The specific interactions of Diph699 with PKI nucleotides are documented at sufficient resolution to support these claims.

results.result: The presence of multiple translocation complexes in a single sample suggests these structures represent equilibrium states of forward and reverse IRES translocation. This is consistent with biochemical studies showing IGR IRESs are prone to reverse translocation and that IRES translocation by eEF2 is futile without aminoacyl-tRNA binding. The similar particle populations suggest energetically similar conformations, though local minima exist for intermediate PKI positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107, C138-C139 combine structural observations with prior biochemical data (C106-C107 cite toe-printing studies). The interpretation that multiple structures represent equilibrium states is reasonable given the experimental design. The energy landscape interpretation (C138-C139) is supported by particle distribution data, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct energy measurements.

results.result: eEF2 directly forces PKI out of the A site through attachment of its histidine-diphthamide tip to PKI's codon-anticodon-like helix. Both PKI and eEF2 passively migrate into P and A sites during spontaneous 40S rotation and head swivel, with eEF2 sliding along the 40S surface through reorganization of electrostatic interactions. Thermal fluctuations of the 40S head are sufficient for translocation along this energetically flat trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C111, C114, C118-C119, C125-C126 present a mechanistic model supported by structural data showing eEF2-PKI interactions and positively charged eEF2 patches sliding over rRNA. The passive migration model is consistent with the structural observations and thermodynamic principles. However, the claim about thermal fluctuations being 'sufficient' (C126) is an inference from observing multiple conformations rather than direct measurement of dynamics.

results.result: This work provides the first high-resolution view of ribosomal translocase dynamics inferred from an ensemble of structures sampled under uniform conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by the novelty of obtaining five near-atomic resolution structures from a single specimen, representing different translocation states. The comparison with prior work (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) shows that previous studies captured only early or late states, not the intermediate states shown here. This represents a significant methodological and scientific advance.

results.result: The structural arrangement of diphthamide in the PKI minor groove rationalizes eEF2 inactivation by diphtheria toxin. ADP-ribosylation at the NE2 position would disrupt diphthamide-PKI interaction, preventing eEF2 from binding the A site or causing non-productive stalling.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 provide a structural rationalization for a well-established biochemical phenomenon (diphtheria toxin inactivation). The structural data showing diphthamide's NE2 atom interacting with PKI supports the mechanistic explanation. This is a reasonable inference connecting structure to prior functional data, though direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanism is not provided.

results.result: tRNA and IRES translocations occur via the same general trajectory, with intermediate A-to-P translocating tRNA positions likely similar to those of PKI in these structures. The TSV IRES structurally and dynamically represents a chimera of the 2tRNA•mRNA complex but lacks three of six tRNA-like domains. The uniformity of ribosome dynamics underscores that translocation is an inherent, structurally-optimized ribosome property.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135, C140-C142 make comparative interpretations connecting IRES and tRNA translocation mechanisms. These are well-supported by structural comparisons with tRNA-bound structures and by the observation that ribosome conformational changes are similar in both systems. The interpretation is strengthened by correlations with prior FRET and biochemical data on tRNA translocation.

results.result: Intergenic IRESs represent a striking example of convergent molecular evolution, where viral mRNAs evolved an atypical structure to employ inherent ribosome dynamics and hijack the host translational machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C144 present an evolutionary interpretation of the structural findings. This is well-supported by the demonstration that the IRES exploits conserved ribosome dynamics without requiring the full complement of tRNA-like features. The convergent evolution interpretation is reasonable given that IGR IRESs can even function on bacterial ribosomes (C12), indicating exploitation of universally conserved ribosome properties.

results.result: Upon translocation, the GCU start codon is positioned in the A site, ready for interaction with Ala-tRNAAla upon eEF2 departure.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is directly supported by structural data in Structure V showing the first ORF codon in the A site (C98). This represents the expected outcome of successful translocation and sets up the next step of translation elongation.

results.result: Background claims about IRES-mediated translation, IGR IRES mechanisms, and translocation requirements including eEF2, intersubunit rotation, hybrid tRNA states, and head swivel, based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C24, C50-C51, C56, and C75 represent established knowledge from prior work, appropriately cited throughout the introduction. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current structural findings. The citations appear accurate and appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Materials and methods: 80S ribosomes from S. cerevisiae W303, His6-tagged eEF2 from yeast TKY675 cells, cryo-EM data collected on FEI Krios at 300 kV, 1,105,737 particles picked automatically, and FREALIGN v9 used for structure determination.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 describe the experimental materials and methods, which are standard and well-documented in the Materials and Methods section. The approaches are appropriate for the study and sufficient detail is provided for reproducibility.
